questions.prompt: What is the chapter's core definition of branding?
choices: A product becomes famous enough that everyone recognizes it
Customers pay more for an objectively similar offering because historical signals have shaped expectation and feeling
A company uses distinctive packaging and design to stand out visually

explanation.gentle: The chapter cares about a premium on a similar offer, not just about attention or style.
explanation.direct: Branding exists here when history changes willingness to pay.
explanation.competitive: No premium on similar substance, no strategic proof.

questions.prompt: Why are time and uncertainty the barrier in this chapter?
choices: Because rivals cannot legally advertise in the same way
Because customers need time to forget the incumbent's product quality
Because rivals cannot quickly copy years of earned trust and meaning

explanation.gentle: A challenger can copy surface cues faster than it can copy built-up confidence.
explanation.direct: Time matters because historical trust cannot be compressed into a quick imitation.
explanation.competitive: The rival can steal the look before it steals the belief.

questions.prompt: Which result best separates awareness from real brand power?
choices: A campaign gets noticed, but customers still refuse to pay more for a similar offer
A brand receives more likes on social media than its rival
A logo becomes easier to recognize from far away

explanation.gentle: Attention alone is not enough if the willingness-to-pay premium does not appear.
explanation.direct: The missing premium shows that visibility has not become the chapter's form of power.
explanation.competitive: The spotlight is bright, but the moat is thin.

questions.prompt: Maya's company just had a successful campaign. What should she test before calling the result brand power?
choices: Whether customers will still pay more when the offer is compared with similar alternatives after the excitement fades
Whether the company can post more frequently than rivals
Whether the campaign visuals are harder for rivals to imitate

explanation.gentle: The premium has to survive beyond the attention spike.
explanation.direct: Brand power requires willingness to pay above similar alternatives, not just temporary buzz.
explanation.competitive: When the noise fades, the price test starts.

questions.prompt: At Priya's campus cafe, two drinks are very similar, yet students still pay a bit more for the established option. What does that most likely show?
choices: Scale economies
Branding through trust and expectation on a similar offer
Switching costs because students cannot change drinks easily

explanation.gentle: The key clue is a premium on a similar option because one choice feels more trusted.
explanation.direct: When offers are close, a higher price tied to expectation points toward branding.
explanation.competitive: The extra charge is coming from belief, not from product distance.

questions.prompt: Which statement best fits the chapter's view of strong brands?
choices: One strong brand should eventually eliminate all other brands in its category
Several strong brands can coexist because each can build its own trust and meaning
A strong brand matters only when customers are locked in by switching costs

explanation.gentle: The chapter explicitly allows more than one brand to stay strong.
explanation.direct: Branding is not exclusive by default because several brands can build distinct trust pools.
explanation.competitive: Strong does not automatically mean solitary.

questions.prompt: Lena notices she accepts a slightly higher price at one local shop after many reliable experiences. What changed?
choices: The shop developed network economies
Historical signals changed her willingness to pay for a similar offer
The shop cornered a scarce resource

explanation.gentle: Repeated reliability changed expectation and made the premium feel acceptable.
explanation.direct: The customer's history with the shop created brand value by lifting price tolerance.
explanation.competitive: Reliability taught her to pay for belief.

questions.prompt: Why might a copied campaign still fail to erase an incumbent's brand power?
choices: Because customers care only about originality in ads
Because campaign mechanics matter less than the trust and association earned over time
Because legal protection always blocks imitation

explanation.gentle: The copied surface may not carry the same earned confidence.
explanation.direct: Brand power survives when the imitator still lacks the historical trust behind the presentation.
explanation.competitive: The rival stole the costume and missed the authority.

questions.prompt: When would branding be weaker under this chapter's logic?
choices: When customers can compare quality instantly and uncertainty is low
When the brand uses a simpler visual identity
When the company operates in more than one market

explanation.gentle: If customers can verify quality immediately, historical signals have less work to do.
explanation.direct: Branding weakens when low uncertainty reduces the value of accumulated trust and expectation.
explanation.competitive: When the proof is instant, the old belief earns less extra rent.

questions.prompt: This chapter's edge comes from willingness to pay shaped by trust and meaning. What would signal the next chapter's barrier instead?
choices: Customers stay because leaving would destroy built-up continuity value
A firm gains preferential access on attractive terms to a scarce resource that independently matters
More users make the product more valuable for other users

explanation.gentle: The next chapter turns to cornered resource, where the edge comes from scarce access rather than perception.
explanation.direct: The barrier shifts from customer expectation to privileged control of an important input.
explanation.competitive: Next, the moat sits in what the firm can get, not in what customers feel.
